body.text: NSW gets modern slavery taskforce in wake of Anti-Slavery Commissioner's report
In short:
Supermarkets and the NSW government have reacted to a new report from the state's Anti-Slavery Commissioner, which alleged illegal activity from labour hire syndicates.
The NSW government has announced a new modern slavery taskforce to share information between agencies.
What's next?
Political and industry figures are calling for state licensing of labour hire firms.

As the NSW government forms a taskforce to investigate modern slavery, the ABC has learnt compliance checks by supermarket giant Woolworths uncovered more than $100,000 in underpayments to workers by its fruit and vegetable suppliers in the past financial year.

The taskforce was announced just days after the NSW Anti-Slavery Commissioner's response to a parliamentary inquiry into modern slavery was tabled, alleging some labour hire syndicates were involved in criminal activities.

James Cockayne's report detailed how they skirted around enforcement and avoided inspections, confirming to the ABC those allegations had been referred to the Australian Federal Police and NSW Police.

The report, which criticised police for taking a reactive approach to labour hire syndicates, recommended that organisations review their supply chains for any connection to the businesses identified.
Woolies orders payments after discovery
Woolworths told the ABC it had this year extended its human rights checks beyond its direct suppliers to the growers who supply them.
A spokesperson said in a statement that, when problems were found, Woolworths could oversee repayments to workers by suppliers, set suppliers deadlines to fix issues, or end a supply relationship.
"As a result of our compliance initiatives in [the 2025-26 financial year], more than $100,000 was returned to workers in our fruit and vegetable supply chain," they said.
"We also run a 'Speak Up' line and encourage workers to contact Woolworths directly about any concerns over their workplace and conditions.
"Where any issue is reported to us, we investigate and take action."
Coles also issued a statement to the ABC saying it did "not tolerate any forms of worker exploitation".
"Compliance with Coles' Ethical Sourcing Policy and applicable workplace laws is a condition of trade for suppliers," a spokesperson said.
Taskforce announced
The NSW government today announced a Modern Slavery Taskforce to bring together state agencies, regulatory bodies and law enforcement agencies.
Members will be drawn from state agencies of NSW Police, SafeWork, industrial relations, the Department of Communities and Justice, local councils and the Migrant Workers Centre.
Federal representatives from the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations and Fair Work Ombudsman will also be invited to join.
NSW Industrial Relations Minister Sophie Cotsis said the taskforce would ensure "better coordination between agencies and law enforcement bodies to stamp out the exploitation of migrant workers".
The government has also promised, if re-elected next year, to introduce a labour hire licensing scheme and require all businesses to use only licensed providers.
Queensland, Victoria, South Australia and the ACT already have labour hire licensing schemes.
Dr Cockayne welcomed the taskforce decision, saying there were "a number of labour hire syndicates exploiting migrant workers in rural and regional NSW".
He has estimated there are 16,400 victims of modern slavery in NSW.
Berry industry welcomes oversight
Berries Australia chief executive Rachel Mackenzie said the taskforce could help enforce criminal laws until all political parties committed to state regulation of labour hire.
She said there was no shortage of intelligence about abuse of workers, but enforcement was lacking.
"Having the police involved in this taskforce is a positive step," Ms Mackenzie said.
"We need multi-agency, joined-up enforcement in the regions.
"We would call on all sides of politics within NSW to put their foot on the sticky paper and back a labour hire licensing scheme."
Brooke Lord, advocacy spokesperson for the Recruitment, Consulting and Staffing Association, said the labour hire industry welcomed the taskforce.
"It frustrates us no end that these kinds of activities continue to operate under the radar," she said.
"Anything that will help us identify these people and stamp out this behaviour is a welcome development."
Ms Lord said the taskforce needed to hold the wider supply chain accountable.
"We do have people who continue to buy services from people who are less expensive in market, who persist in creating a market for these dodgy operators," she said.
"I really hope that the actions of the taskforce will [target] the dodgy operators, but also those people who are buying services they know probably don't smell quite right."
People 'flying under the radar'
Modern Slavery Committee chair Joe McGirr said the taskforce was a positive step, as government agencies have operated in silos for too long.
"One of the issues that was a concern to the committee has been the sharing of information between different government departments," he said.
"Perpetrators of modern slavery, disreputable labour hire firms and people flying under the radar, have often been able to escape detection.
"The key issue is the labour hire regulation, and I think there is a strong bipartisan support for it," he said.
